Pulling The REINS: Training-Free Safety Alignment of Video Diffusion Models via Representation Steering

Rohit Kundu Affiliation: University of California, Riverside    Arindam Dutta Affiliation: University of California, Riverside    Sarosij Bose Affiliation: University of California, Riverside    Athula Balachandran Affiliation: YouTube (Google)    Amit K. Roy-Chowdhury Affiliation: University of California, Riverside
Abstract

Open-weight video diffusion models can generate photorealistic unsafe content, from violence to misinformation, yet existing defenses either require expensive safety fine-tuning that degrades general capability, or apply external filters that are trivially bypassed by adversarial prompts. We present REINS (REpresentation-space INference-time Safety steering), a training-free method that aligns video diffusion models at inference time by steering their internal representations toward safe generation. Our key finding is that safety-relevant structure is linearly encoded in the hidden-state activations of video diffusion transformers, and a single direction, discovered via Supervised PCA on binary safety labels, suffices to separate safe from unsafe generation trajectories. At inference, adding this direction to hidden states at an intermediate transformer layer redirects generation from harmful content to semantically related safe alternatives, with no weight updates, no concept enumeration, and negligible computational overhead. Through mechanistic analysis, we reveal that while safety information accumulates monotonically with transformer depth, steering effectiveness peaks at intermediate layers (∼50%{\sim}50\% depth), exposing a fundamental tradeoff between information availability and downstream propagation capacity. We evaluate REINS across 9 video diffusion models, multiple parameter scales (1.3B-5B), and both text-to-video and image-to-video generation, to our knowledge, the broadest safety evaluation suite in the video generation literature.

WARNING: The paper contains content that may be offensive and disturbing in nature.

1 Introduction

The rapid proliferation of open-weight text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] has made high-fidelity video synthesis widely accessible, enabling creative applications from filmmaking to education. However, this accessibility carries a significant risk, as these same models can generate photorealistic videos depicting violence, sexually explicit content, and targeted misinformation with minimal effort [1, 8, 2]. Unlike their proprietary counterparts [9, 10, 11], most open-weight models lack built-in safety mechanisms, and the few that do [12] require extensive safety-specific fine-tuning, which in turn demands large-scale annotated datasets, significant computational resources, and risks degrading general-purpose generation quality.

Existing algorithms for preventing unsafe video generation operate at two fundamentally limited extremes. Prompt-level filtering [13, 14] blocks generation before it begins by classifying input prompts as safe or unsafe. While simple to deploy, these methods are trivially circumvented through prompt jailbreaking [15, 16], indirect phrasing, and adversarial rewording. At the other extreme, output-level filtering [17, 18] screens generated videos post-hoc and discards unsafe ones, wasting the full computational cost of generation and still leaves the model exploitable. Importantly, an adversary can bypass the filtering processes by manual intervention or adversarial prompting. Crucially, neither approach engages with the generation process itself, the model’s internal representations continue to encode and propagate unsafe content through every transformer block and denoising step, regardless of whether the resulting video is ultimately shown or suppressed. This motivates a fundamentally different approach: rather than gating inputs or outputs, intervene within generation to steer the model’s computations toward safe outputs before they are ever decoded into pixels.

In this paper, we show that such an intervention is remarkably effective: without modifying any model architecture or weights, and without relying on external filters, the video diffusion model (VDM) can be steered to generate safe outputs irrespective of input prompts. Our key observation is that the hidden-state activations at intermediate layers of VDMs encode a linearly separable representation of whether the video being generated is safe or unsafe, even in the early stages of the denoising process, well before the final output is decoded. This structure can be identified through a lightweight offline calibration using only a pretrained safety classifier and Supervised Principal Component Analysis (SPCA) [19], yielding a single direction in the activation space that maximally separates safe from unsafe generation trajectories. At inference time, a simple additive perturbation along this direction steers the model’s internal representations toward the safe subspace, redirecting generation from harmful content to semantically related but safe alternatives.

Building on this insight, we propose REINS (REpresentation-space INference-time Safety steering), a training-free safety alignment method for VDMs. At inference, REINS adds a single precomputed direction (scaled by a model-adaptive strength) to the hidden states of an intermediate transformer layer during the first half of the denoising process, with per-channel norm preservation to prevent cross-channel coupling artifacts and consistent application across both classifier-free guidance branches. The steering direction is obtained from a lightweight offline procedure that uses only forward passes through the model with no backpropagation, no gradient computation, no weight updates, and no training data beyond a small set of prompts. As summarized in Fig. 1, REINS directly manipulates internal hidden states to steer generation from harmful to safe content without requiring any weight updates. We situate REINS among existing analogous algorithms, summarizing key differences in Table 1, with a detailed discussion on related works available in appendix §A.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce REINS, the first training-free, inference-time safety alignment method for video diffusion models. Unlike latent-space steering approaches [20], REINS operates on the semantically structured hidden-state representations of diffusion models, where safety-relevant features are linearly accessible, a property we verify does not hold in latent-space for video models.

  • •

    We provide a mechanistic analysis of safety representations in VDMs, revealing that (a) safety-relevant information, as measured by HSIC, accumulates monotonically with transformer depth, yet (b) steering effectiveness peaks at intermediate layers (∼50%{\sim}50\% depth), exposing a fundamental tradeoff between information availability and downstream propagation capacity. This analysis yields a principled, data-driven layer selection procedure.

  • •

    We demonstrate the generalizability of REINS across multiple model architectures (CogVideoX [3], Wan 2.1 [4], Allegro [7]), scales (1.3B-5B parameters), generation paradigms (T2V and I2V), and two independent safety classifiers (in-domain and OOD) on two distinct datasets.

  • •

    We propose a cross-model steering calibration heuristic based on activation norms that allows practitioners to estimate the appropriate steering strength for a new model from its activation statistics, without exhaustive hyperparameter search.

2 Method

2.1 Preliminaries

Latent video diffusion: Video diffusion models (VDMs) generate a video 𝐯∈ℝF×H×W×3\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times H\times W\times 3} conditioned on an input cc, such as text, images, or other control signals. Modern VDMs operate in the latent space of a variational autoencoder [3, 5]. An encoder ℰ\mathcal{E} maps the video to a latent 𝐱0=ℰ⁡(𝐯)∈ℝC×F′×H′×W′\mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times F^{\prime}\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}}, where F′=⌈F/τ⌉F^{\prime}=\lceil F/\tau\rceil denotes the temporally compressed length and H′=H/sH^{\prime}=H/s, W′=W/sW^{\prime}=W/s denote the spatially compressed resolution. A decoder 𝒟\mathcal{D} maps the final latent back to pixel space.

The forward diffusion process corrupts a clean latent 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} into Gaussian noise:

q⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱0)=𝒩⁡(𝐱t,α¯t​𝐱0,(1−α¯t)​𝐈),q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t};\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{x}_{0},(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\mathbf{I}\right), (1)

where {α¯t}t=1T\{\bar{\alpha}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} is a predefined noise schedule. A neural network ϵθ​(𝐱t,t,c)\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,c) is trained to predict the noise component by minimizing

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼𝐱0,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(𝐱t,t,c)‖22],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t}\left[\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,c)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (2)

with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and 𝐱t=α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}. At inference, generation starts from Gaussian noise and proceeds by iterative denoising:

𝐱t−1=μθ​(𝐱t,t,c)+σt​𝐳,𝐳∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈),\mathbf{x}_{t-1}=\mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,c)+\sigma_{t}\mathbf{z},\qquad\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), (3)

where μθ\mu_{\theta} is determined by the chosen sampler and depends on the model prediction. After denoising, the latent is decoded as 𝐯=𝒟⁡(𝐱0)\mathbf{v}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x}_{0}).

Transformer hidden states: Modern VDMs [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] commonly instantiate ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} as a transformer architecture (DiTs) over spatio-temporal latent tokens. The latent 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is patch-embedded into S=F′​H^​W^S=F^{\prime}\hat{H}\hat{W} tokens of dimension DD, where H^=H′/p\hat{H}=H^{\prime}/p and W^=W′/p\hat{W}=W^{\prime}/p for spatial patch size pp. These tokens are processed by LL transformer blocks. We denote the hidden state at the output of block l∈{0,…,L−1}l\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\} and denoising timestep tt as 𝐡l(t)∈ℝS×D.\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D}. The final block output is projected back to latent dimensions to produce the model prediction. In this work, we intervene on these intermediate hidden states 𝐡l(t)\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(t)}, which encode the model’s fused representation of the current noisy latent, timestep, and conditioning input before it is decoded to a corresponding video.

Classifier-free guidance: VDMs often use classifier-free guidance (CFG) [26] to improve adherence to the conditioning input. At each denoising step, the model is evaluated once with the condition cc and once with the null condition ∅\varnothing, and the two predictions are combined as

ϵ~θ​(𝐱t,t,c)=ϵθ​(𝐱t,t,∅)+w⁡[ϵθ​(𝐱t,t,c)−ϵθ​(𝐱t,t,∅)],\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,c)=\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\varnothing)+w\left[\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\varnothing)\right], (4)

where w≥1w\geq 1 is the guidance scale. The guided prediction ϵ~θ\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta} is then used in the reverse update. Since CFG requires both conditional and unconditional forward passes, any hidden-state intervention must be applied consistently to both branches.

Safety Classifier: We assume access to a safety classifier f:ℝF×H×W×3→[0,1]f:\mathbb{R}^{F\times H\times W\times 3}\rightarrow[0,1] that assigns a safety score to a generated video. Given a threshold γ\gamma, we define the binary label y=𝟏{f(𝐯)>γ},y=\mathbf{1}\{f(\mathbf{v})>\gamma\}, where y=1y=1 denotes a safe generation. The classifier is used only during a one-time calibration phase to label generated videos; it is not required during deployment.

2.2 Safety Steering in Representation Space

We align video diffusion models with safety constraints by intervening directly on their internal representations during sampling. Our method is based on the hypothesis that safety-relevant behavior is linearly accessible in the hidden states of a video diffusion transformer. In particular, we seek an intermediate layer whose activations separate safe and unsafe generations along a low-dimensional direction, analogous to representation-space steering observed for high-level concepts in language models [27, 28, 29]. We empirically validate this hypothesis for video diffusion models in Sec. 3.2.

Let 𝐡l(t)∈ℝS×D\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D} denote the hidden state at transformer layer ll and denoising timestep tt. We aim to identify an intervention layer l∗l^{*} and a unit-norm steering direction 𝜹∈ℝD\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} such that adding 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} to the hidden representation biases generation toward safer outputs. The basic intervention takes the form

𝐡~l∗(t)=𝐡l∗(t)+λ⋅𝜹,\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l^{*}}^{(t)}=\mathbf{h}_{l^{*}}^{(t)}+\lambda\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta}, (5)

where λ>0\lambda>0 controls the steering strength and the direction 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} is broadcast across the spatio-temporal token dimension. Geometrically, this assumes that safe and unsafe generations induce separable activation patterns at some intermediate layer and that moving hidden states along the separating direction can influence the denoising trajectory.

Although Eq. 5 has a simple additive form, applying it effectively requires determining three quantities: the intervention layer l∗l^{*}, the steering direction 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} and the steering strength λ\lambda. The next section describes how we use Supervised-PCA (SPCA) [19] based representation [19] probing to discover the optimal candidate safety directions and to select the optimal intervention layer. We then describe how the resulting intervention is applied during inference in Sec. 2.4.

2.3 SPCA-Based Discovery of Safety Directions and Intervention Layers

We next describe how REINS calibrates the steering direction and the intervention layer using a small held-out set. Calibration is performed once per model and is reused thereafter: for each transformer layer l∈{0,…,L−1}l\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}, SPCA yields a candidate direction 𝜹l\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l} and a layer-wise spectrum whose eigenvalue mass measures linearly accessible safety structures.

Calibration set: We generate NN videos {𝐯(i)}i=1N\{\mathbf{v}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} from safety-critical conditioning inputs {c(i)}i=1N\{c^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} using the base VDM. Each generated video is assigned a binary safety label y(i)∈{0,1}y^{(i)}\in\{0,1\} using the safety classifier defined in Sec. 2.1, where y(i)=1y^{(i)}=1 denotes a safe generation. During generation, we record the hidden-state activations 𝐡l(i,k)∈ℝS×D\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(i,k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D} for each candidate layer ll and denoising iteration kk. We define the set of early denoising iterations used for probing and steering as 𝒦steer={1,…,⌊α​T⌋},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{steer}}=\{1,\ldots,\lfloor\alpha T\rfloor\}, with steering fraction α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1].

Temporal-spatial aggregation: For each layer ll, video ii, and denoising iteration kk, we summarize the hidden state by averaging over its SS spatio-temporal tokens (Eq. 6), and then average these token-pooled representations over the early denoising iterations (Eq. 7):

𝐡¯l(i,k)=1S​∑j=1S𝐡l,j(i,k)∈ℝD,\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{l}^{(i,k)}=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{j=1}^{S}\mathbf{h}_{l,j}^{(i,k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (6)
𝐫l(i)=1|𝒦steer|​∑k∈𝒦steer𝐡¯l(i,k)∈ℝD.\mathbf{r}_{l}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{steer}}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{steer}}}\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{l}^{(i,k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. (7)

where 𝐡l,j(i,k)∈ℝD\mathbf{h}_{l,j}^{(i,k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denotes the hidden vector of token jj. Each generated video is represented by a single vector 𝐫l(i)\mathbf{r}_{l}^{(i)} at layer ll. We stack these vectors to form

𝐑l=[(𝐫l(1))⊤;…;(𝐫l(N))⊤]∈ℝN×D.\mathbf{R}_{l}=\big[(\mathbf{r}_{l}^{(1)})^{\top};\ldots;(\mathbf{r}_{l}^{(N)})^{\top}\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}. (8)

and construct the one-hot label matrix 𝐘∈ℝN×2\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2} from the binary safety labels {y(i)}i=1N\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}.

SPCA objective: For a candidate layer ll, we seek a direction 𝐮∈ℝD\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} such that the projected representations 𝐑l​𝐮\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u} are maximally dependent on the safety labels. We measure this dependence using HSIC [30] and adopt the supervised PCA (SPCA) formulation of [19]. Additional derivation details are provided in appendix §B.

Let 𝐇=𝐈N−1N​𝟏N​𝟏N⊤\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{I}_{N}-\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top} denote the centering matrix and 𝐊Y​Y=𝐘𝐘⊤\mathbf{K}_{YY}=\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}^{\top} the label kernel. SPCA reduces to the constrained eigenvalue problem to:

max𝐮𝐮⊤​𝐀l​𝐮,s.t.‖𝐮‖2=1,\max_{\mathbf{u}}\quad\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{l}\mathbf{u},\qquad\mathrm{s.t.}\quad\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}=1, (9)
𝐀l=𝐑l⊤​𝐇𝐊Y​Y​𝐇𝐑l∈ℝD×D.\mathbf{A}_{l}=\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{K}_{YY}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{R}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}. (10)

The top eigenvector of 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l} gives the direction of maximum label-dependent variance at layer ll.

Candidate safety direction: For each layer ll, we define the candidate safety direction as the top eigenvector of the SPCA matrix: 𝜹l=eigvec1​(𝐀l)\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}=\mathrm{eigvec}_{1}(\mathbf{A}_{l}). We orient the direction so that safe generations have larger projection values than unsafe generations:

1|𝒮|​∑i∈𝒮⟨𝜹l,𝐫l(i)⟩>1|𝒰|​∑i∈𝒰⟨𝜹l,𝐫l(i)⟩,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\left\langle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l},\mathbf{r}_{l}^{(i)}\right\rangle>\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{U}}\left\langle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l},\mathbf{r}_{l}^{(i)}\right\rangle, (11)

where 𝒮={i:y(i)=1}\mathcal{S}=\{i:y^{(i)}=1\} and 𝒰={i:y(i)=0}\mathcal{U}=\{i:y^{(i)}=0\}. If this inequality is not satisfied, we replace 𝜹l\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l} with −𝜹l-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}.

Layer-wise safety structure: The eigenvalue spectrum of 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l} provides a diagnostic for how strongly safety-relevant information is linearly represented at layer ll. We define the SPCA score sl=∑m=1kσl(m)s_{l}=\sum_{m=1}^{k}\sigma_{l}^{(m)}, where σl(m)\sigma_{l}^{(m)} is the mm-th largest eigenvalue of 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l}. Intuitively, sls_{l} measures the amount of label-dependent variance captured by the top-kk supervised components at layer ll.

Selecting the intervention layer: The SPCA score identifies where safety information is linearly accessible, but information content alone does not determine whether an intervention will be effective. Very shallow layers may not yet encode safety-relevant semantics, whereas very deep layers may leave insufficient downstream computation for the perturbation to influence the denoising trajectory. We therefore use the SPCA spectrum as a representation-level diagnostic and select the final intervention layer using a small steering sweep over candidate layers.

For each candidate layer ll, we apply the corresponding direction 𝜹l\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l} during inference and measure both safety rate and generation quality. We select

l∗=arg⁡maxl​SafetyRate​(l)s.t.|VQ⁡(l)−VQbase|≤ϵ;|MQ⁡(l)−MQbase|≤ϵ,l^{*}=\arg\max_{l}\;\mathrm{\texttt{SafetyRate}}(l)\quad\mathrm{s.t.}\quad|\mathrm{VQ}(l)-\mathrm{VQ}_{\mathrm{base}}|\leq\epsilon;|\mathrm{MQ}(l)-\mathrm{MQ}_{\mathrm{base}}|\leq\epsilon, (12)

where ϵ\epsilon controls the allowable degradation in generation quality. Empirically, we observe that the SPCA score tends to increase with depth, indicating that later layers encode stronger safety-relevant structure, while the best safety-quality tradeoff occurs at intermediate layers. This suggests a tradeoff between representation availability and downstream propagation capacity. After selecting l∗l^{*}, the final steering direction is 𝜹=𝜹l∗.\boldsymbol{\delta}=\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l^{*}}.

Rank-1 sufficiency: Although the SPCA spectrum may contain multiple supervised components, we use only the top eigenvector for steering. Empirically, the leading component captures the dominant safe/unsafe separation (verified in Fig. 5), while adding higher components can introduce inter-category variation that weakens the intervention. This rank-1 choice also mirrors prior findings that certain high-level behaviors in large language models can be controlled by a single dominant representation direction [29].

2.4 Inference-Time Safety Steering

Given the intervention layer l∗l^{*} and direction 𝜹=𝜹l∗\boldsymbol{\delta}=\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l^{*}} obtained from the calibration in Sec. 2.3, REINS steers generation by perturbing the hidden states of the diffusion transformer at inference. Model weights, conditioning input, sampler, and decoder remain unchanged.

Hidden-state perturbation: At each early denoising iteration k∈𝒦steerk\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{steer}}, we run the VDM normally up to block l∗l^{*} and add 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} to every spatio-temporal token of the output hidden state:

𝐡~l∗,j(k)=𝐡l∗,j(k)+λ⋅𝜹,j=1,…,S,\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l^{*},j}^{(k)}=\mathbf{h}_{l^{*},j}^{(k)}+\lambda\,\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta},\qquad j=1,\ldots,S, (13)

where λ>0\lambda>0 is the steering strength and 𝜹∈ℝD\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is shared across all tokens. Steering is restricted to the early iterations because they shape global semantics and coarse motion, while later iterations primarily refine local appearance. The remaining iterations proceed unmodified. Transformer blocks beyond l∗l^{*} are evaluated normally to produce the noise prediction.

Per-channel norm preservation: A raw additive perturbation can shift the per-channel scale of the hidden state and produce artifacts such as oversaturation or color drift. We therefore rescale the perturbed activations so that each channel retains its original token-wise ℓ2\ell_{2} norm:

𝐡^l∗(k)=𝐡~l∗(k)⊙‖𝐡l∗(k)‖tok‖𝐡~l∗(k)‖tok+ϵ,\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l^{*}}^{(k)}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l^{*}}^{(k)}\;\odot\;\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{l^{*}}^{(k)}\|_{\mathrm{tok}}}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l^{*}}^{(k)}\|_{\mathrm{tok}}+\epsilon}, (14)

where ∥⋅∥tok∈ℝD\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{tok}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denotes the per-channel ℓ2\ell_{2} norm computed across the SS tokens, ⊙\odot broadcasts the scaling vector across the token dimension. This preserves per-channel energy while allowing the relative activation pattern induced by 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} to propagate to subsequent blocks.

Application under CFG: When classifier-free guidance is enabled, the same perturbation is applied to both the conditional and unconditional branches before the CFG combination in Eq. 4. Steering only one branch introduces a mismatch between the two predictions and degrades visual quality.

Steering Strength Calibration: Different models require different steering magnitudes λ\lambda due to varying activation scales. We propose a simple calibration heuristic based on activation norm and the alignment between hidden states and the steering direction. For a model ℳ\mathcal{M}, we compute the characteristic scale:

ρℳ=𝔼t∈𝒯steer​[‖𝐡¯(t)‖2cos⁡(𝐡¯(t),𝜹)],\rho_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathbb{E}_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{steer}}}\left[\frac{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(t)}\|_{2}}{\cos(\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\delta})}\right], (15)

where the expectation is over denoising steps and calibration videos. Empirically, the optimal λ\lambda follows an approximate power law λ∝ρℳβ\lambda\propto\rho_{\mathcal{M}}^{\beta} with β≈1.3\beta\approx 1.3, enabling practitioners to estimate a suitable λ\lambda from activation statistics alone without exhaustive search (Fig. 5).

3 Experiments

We evaluate REINS across a diverse suite of nine video diffusion models, spanning three architectural families (CogVideoX, Wan, LTX/Mochi/Allegro), parameter scales from 1.3B to 5B, and two generation paradigms, i.e. , T2V (text-to-video) and I2V (image-to-video). To our knowledge, this constitutes the broadest safety evaluation suite in the video generation literature. Additional details are provided in the appendix §C.

Models: We evaluate six text-to-video (T2V) models: CogVideoX-2B, CogVideoX-5B [3], Wan2.1-1.3B [4], Mochi-1 [5], Allegro [7], and LTX-Video [6] and three image-to-video (I2V) models: CogVideoX-5B-I2V [3], LTX-Video-I2V [6], and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [4]. This selection covers widely used open-source video generation models and spans the architectural diversity of the field. Data: We use the SafeSora [1] and SafeWatch-Bench [2] datasets, with evaluation prompts covering all safety categories defined by the respective benchmarks. For each model, identical prompts and random seeds are used for baseline and REINS-steered generation to enable paired comparison. Metrics: We report three metrics: (i) Safety Rate (↑\uparrow), the fraction of generated videos classified as safe by the safety classifier; (ii) Visual Quality (VQ) [31] (↑\uparrow); and (iii) Motion Quality (MQ) [31] (↑\uparrow), where VQ and MQ are measured as win rates of REINS-steered generations against baseline generations under the VideoAlign reward model, with 50% indicating parity. We additionally report safety results using an OOD classifier (model trained on SafeWatch-Bench [2], used on SafeSora [1] and vice versa).

3.1 Results

Safety Boost: Table 2 presents our main quantitative results. REINS improves safety on every one of the nine models across both benchmarks, with mean gains of +0.22 on SafeSora and +0.21 on SafeWatch-Bench. The improvement holds across three architectural families, scales from 1.3B to 5B parameters, and both T2V and I2V generation paradigms, without any per-model retraining. This breadth of generalization confirms that the safety direction discovered by SPCA captures a representational structure shared across the video diffusion transformer family rather than a model-specific artifact. The improvement is most pronounced under conditions where unsafe generation is most prevalent. On SafeWatch-Bench, where baselines produce safe content as little as 3% of the time (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B), REINS delivers gains of up to +0.52 (LTX-Video-I2V), demonstrating that representation-space steering remains effective precisely where prompt distributions are most adversarial.

Quality Preservation: Quality is preserved alongside these safety gains. Across both benchmarks, REINS achieves win rates against the baseline that are at-or-above parity on motion quality for the majority of models (mean MQ of 49.2% on SafeSora, 61.9% on SafeWatch), with visual quality in a competitive band (mean VQ of 38.9% and 47.4% respectively). On SafeWatch-Bench in particular, where baselines frequently exhibit incoherent motion as a byproduct of executing adversarial prompts, steering toward the safe manifold incidentally improves motion quality. Fig. 2 illustrates this redirection across the major SafeSora [1] safety categories. Two properties are consistently visible: scene composition is preserved, and plausible safe narratives emerge from the model’s own priors rather than from the noise or solid-color collapse characteristic of naïve activation addition. This is the behavior the SPCA objective targets by construction, the discovered direction separates safe from unsafe trajectories within the representation space the model already uses.

Comparison with Baselines: We compare REINS against two representative baselines on Wan2.1-1.3B [4]: (i) noise-space steering, where the same SPCA formulation we use for 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} is applied to the noise-space latent 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} rather than to hidden states (PolyJuice [20]-style [details in appendix §D] and (ii) LlamaPromptGuard-2 [32] [details in appendix §C.5] representing the dominant deployed defense. To probe robustness, we additionally evaluate the filtering baseline and REINS under adversarial prompts from MMA-Diffusion [33]. REINS is applied zero-shot: 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} remains the direction calibrated on SafeSora [1] and is not refit to the attack distribution, testing whether safety is captured as a property of the representation space invariant to prompt surface form. Table 3 summarizes the results. Three observations follow. First, the noise-space variant of our SPCA direction yields no measurable safety gain and collapses generation quality to single digits on VQ and MQ, confirming that safety is a semantic property of the transformer’s hidden states, not a statistical property of the noise-space latent. Second, prompt filtering improves safety on standard prompts (0.52 →\to 0.67) but its safety rate collapses under MMA-Diffusion [15], while REINS performance increases (0.72 →\to 0.79). The asymmetry is structural: filters reason about prompt surface form, which adversaries can perturb; REINS reasons about the hidden-state representation downstream of prompt encoding, which the attack does not control. Third, REINS is the only method that preserves quality (VQ ≥50\geq 50, MQ ≥80\geq 80) in both regimes, whereas filtering depresses quality through blocked outputs, and noise-space steering destroys it.

3.2 Discussion

The results in Sec. 3.1 establish that REINS works. The analyses below establish why, by testing the structural assumptions the method depends on. Representation-space steering is only coherent if (a) safety is linearly accessible at a specific layer rather than diffusely distributed, (b) the steering strength required to act on this structure is predictable from the model rather than hyperparameter-tuned per setting, (c) the safety subspace is low-dimensional rather than requiring high-rank intervention, and (d) the resulting safety improvements arise from a genuine representational shift rather than generation collapse or classifier-specific artifacts. Each of the four analyses that follow targets one of these assumptions; together they ground REINS in a falsifiable account of how representation-space safety steering operates in VDMs.

Effective steering range across layers: Fig. 3 shows that effective steering occurs at intermediate layers: safety improves while quality is preserved, whereas early layers lack semantic safety features and late-layer steering collapses generation, a pattern consistent across in-domain and OOD classifiers. This highlights that the intervention site is as important as the direction itself. Noise-space steering acts before semantic fusion and fails in Sec. 3.1; prompt interventions are similarly indirect, output filtering is post-hoc, and weight-level erasure [22, 23] requires parameter changes tied to predefined concepts. Hidden states provide the natural intervention point: conditioning has been integrated into a semantic representation, but the denoising prediction has not yet been fixed.

Steering strength calibration: Fig. 5 shows that the optimal steering strength varies by orders of magnitude across models (λ=3\lambda{=}3 for Allegro, λ=410\lambda{=}410 for CogVideoX-5B-I2V). However, λ\lambda follows a predictable power-law relationship with the ratio ρ=‖h‖/cos⁡(h,δ)\rho=\|h\|/\cos(h,\delta), where hh is the hidden-state norm and δ\delta is the safety direction. This allows fast calibration on new models using a single sample rather than a full hyperparameter sweep.

Safety direction rank: Fig. 5 ablates the rank of the steering subspace. A rank-1 direction, a single vector, captures approximately 68% of the safety-relevant variance and saturates safety rate at ∼\sim0.98 with sufficient λ\lambda. Higher ranks marginally improve safety but at a steeper VQ/MQ cost. This is the video-domain analogue of the one-dimensional refusal finding in LLMs [29] and confirms that safety, at the representation level, is a low-dimensional property of video diffusion transformers.

Steering shift analysis: Fig. 6 visualizes the effect of steering directly on the hidden-state representations. The projection of hidden states onto the safety direction shifts cleanly from a bimodal unsafe/safe distribution at baseline to a unimodal safe distribution under steering. This demonstrates that our intervention acts on the representation in the predicted direction, and critically, that this representational shift faithfully translates into the classifier-visible safety property of the generated video.

4 Conclusion

We introduced REINS, a training-free method for aligning video diffusion models with safety constraints by steering internal representations at inference time. We find that safety is linearly encoded in VDM hidden states: a single SPCA direction from binary safety labels redirects harmful generations toward semantically related safe alternatives, without weight updates, concept enumeration, or meaningful overhead. Across 9 open-weight VDMs spanning three architectural families, two scales, and both T2V and I2V settings, REINS consistently improves safety on two benchmarks while preserving quality and remaining robust to adversarial prompts where prompt-level filtering fails.
Limitations and future directions: REINS relies on a linear dependence between hidden-state activations and safety labels via SPCA; cases where safety is nonlinearly encoded would require a nonlinear kernel formulation, along with the added complexity of solving a pre-video problem to map the nonlinear embedding back to the activation space. Extending REINS to other forms of behavioral alignment beyond binary safety, such as fairness, factuality, or stylistic constraints, is a promising direction.
Ethical considerations: While REINS is designed to make VDMs safer, the same representation-space framework could, in principle, be inverted to suppress safe content or amplify unsafe content given an adversarial calibration set. REINS is intended solely for responsible safety alignment of open-weight video diffusion models, and we strongly oppose its use for malicious purposes. We do not release calibration sets containing unsafe generations, and we discuss defense mechanisms against potential misuse in the appendix §E.

Appendix

Appendix A Related Work

Prompt and output filtering: The most common defenses operate outside the generative model. Prompt-level classifiers [13, 34] block unsafe inputs before generation, while output-level checkers [21] suppress unsafe samples after they are produced. These methods are simple and modular, but they do not alter the model’s internal generation trajectory. As a result, they are vulnerable to adversarial prompting: SneakyPrompt [35] bypasses text and image safety filters through RL-guided token perturbations, and MMA-Diffusion [15] extends such attacks to multimodal systems. For video, T2VSafetyBench [36] shows that temporally composing individually benign prompts can still yield unsafe videos, highlighting a modality-specific weakness of prompt-only defenses.

Concept unlearning: Another line of work modifies model weights to remove targeted unsafe concepts [22, 23, 37, 38, 39]. ESD [22] fine-tunes cross-attention layers to suppress specified concepts, while UCE [23] supports simultaneous editing of multiple concepts. Although these methods intervene more directly than filtering, they remain limited in three ways: they require enumerating the concepts to erase, unlearned concepts can be recovered through lightweight fine-tuning [40, 41], and existing methods are designed primarily for image diffusion UNets. Extending concept erasure to video diffusion transformers while preserving temporal coherence remains largely unexplored.

Inference-time safety alignment: Training-free inference-time methods improve safety during generation without modifying weights. Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [24] applies negative classifier-free guidance toward textual safety concepts such as “nudity” or “violence,” but remains limited by text specifications and the conditioning pathway that adversarial prompts can exploit. Li et al. [25] discover interpretable UNet bottleneck directions via self-supervised reconstruction but require per-concept gradient optimization. PolyJuice [20] uses Supervised PCA, the core formulation we adopt, to find directions in the noise-space latent of text-to-image diffusion models for detector evasion. In contrast, we show that noise-space steering is insufficient for high-level video safety alignment and instead intervene in transformer hidden states. Video diffusion adds temporal challenges as representations evolve across denoising steps, steering must remain frame-coherent, and naive perturbations can introduce artifacts. To our knowledge, REINS is the first training-free safety alignment method for video diffusion models.

Appendix B Derivation of the SPCA Objective

In Sec. 2.3 of the main paper, we stated the SPCA objective as a constrained eigenvalue problem (Eqs. 9-10). For completeness, we provide the derivation from the underlying HSIC criterion and document the practical computational shortcut used to compute the steering direction efficiently for high-dimensional hidden states.

HSIC criterion and the linear projection.

We seek a direction 𝐮∈ℝD\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} such that the projected representations 𝐑l​𝐮∈ℝN\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} are maximally dependent on the safety labels 𝐘∈ℝN×2\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2}. We measure dependence via the empirical Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) [30]:

HSIC⁡(𝐑l​𝐮,𝐘)=1(N−1)2​tr​(𝐊𝐑l​𝐮​𝐇​𝐊Y​Y​𝐇),\mathrm{HSIC}(\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u},\mathbf{Y})\;=\;\frac{1}{(N-1)^{2}}\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{K}_{YY}\,\mathbf{H}\right), (A1)

where 𝐊𝐑l​𝐮∈ℝN×N\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is the linear-kernel matrix of the projected representations and 𝐊Y​Y=𝐘𝐘⊤\mathbf{K}_{YY}=\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}^{\top} is the label kernel. Because the projection is one-dimensional, the linear kernel takes the rank-one form

𝐊𝐑l​𝐮=(𝐑l​𝐮)​(𝐑l​𝐮)⊤.\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u}}\;=\;(\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u})(\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u})^{\top}. (A2)

Reduction to a quadratic form.

Substituting and applying the cyclic property of the trace yields

HSIC⁡(𝐑l​𝐮,𝐘)∝tr⁡((𝐑l​𝐮)​(𝐑l​𝐮)⊤​𝐇​𝐊Y​Y​𝐇)=𝐮⊤​𝐑l⊤​𝐇​𝐊Y​Y​𝐇​𝐑l​𝐮=𝐮⊤​𝐀l​𝐮,\displaystyle\mathrm{HSIC}(\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u},\mathbf{Y})\;\propto\;\mathrm{tr}\!\left((\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u})(\mathbf{R}_{l}\mathbf{u})^{\top}\,\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{K}_{YY}\,\mathbf{H}\right)\;=\;\mathbf{u}^{\top}\,\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{K}_{YY}\,\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{R}_{l}\,\mathbf{u}\;=\;\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{l}\mathbf{u}, (A3)

recovering Eqs. 9-10 of the main paper, with 𝐀l=𝐑l⊤​𝐇​𝐊Y​Y​𝐇​𝐑l∈ℝD×D\mathbf{A}_{l}=\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{K}_{YY}\,\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{R}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}.

Maximization as a Rayleigh quotient.

Maximizing 𝐮⊤​𝐀l​𝐮\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{l}\mathbf{u} under the unit-norm constraint ‖𝐮‖2=1\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}=1 is a standard Rayleigh quotient problem. The optimum is attained at the top eigenvector of 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l}, with optimal value equal to the largest eigenvalue [42]:

𝜹l=arg⁡max‖𝐮‖2=1​𝐮⊤​𝐀l​𝐮=eigvec1​(𝐀l).\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}\;=\;\arg\max_{\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}=1}\,\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{l}\mathbf{u}\;=\;\mathrm{eigvec}_{1}(\mathbf{A}_{l}). (A4)

Efficient computation via cross-covariance SVD.

For high-dimensional hidden states (D≫ND\gg N, with DD ranging from ∼\sim1920 to ∼\sim4096 and N=500N=500 in our setting), direct eigendecomposition of the D×DD\times D matrix 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l} is computationally wasteful. Because 𝐊Y​Y\mathbf{K}_{YY} has rank at most 22 for binary safety labels, 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l} has rank at most 22, and only its top two eigenvalues are non-zero. Defining the cross-covariance

𝐂l=𝐑l⊤​𝐇​𝐘∈ℝD×2,\mathbf{C}_{l}\;=\;\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\top}\,\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{Y}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{D\times 2}, (A5)

and using the symmetry (𝐇⊤=𝐇\mathbf{H}^{\top}=\mathbf{H}) and idempotence (𝐇𝐇=𝐇\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{H}) of the centering matrix, we have

𝐂l​𝐂l⊤=𝐑l⊤​𝐇​𝐘𝐘⊤​𝐇​𝐑l=𝐑l⊤​𝐇​𝐊Y​Y​𝐇​𝐑l=𝐀l.\mathbf{C}_{l}\mathbf{C}_{l}^{\top}\;=\;\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{R}_{l}\;=\;\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{K}_{YY}\,\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{R}_{l}\;=\;\mathbf{A}_{l}. (A6)

Hence the top eigenvectors of 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l} coincide with the left singular vectors of 𝐂l\mathbf{C}_{l}, and the corresponding eigenvalues are the squared singular values. In practice, we compute 𝜹l\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l} via SVD of the D×2D\times 2 matrix 𝐂l\mathbf{C}_{l}, reducing computational cost from 𝒪⁡(D3)\mathcal{O}(D^{3}) to 𝒪⁡(N​D)\mathcal{O}(ND).

Appendix C Implementation Details

C.1 Resource Details

All video-generation experiments are run on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada (48 GB) GPU, but multi-GPU support has been utilized purely to reduce wall-clock time, and is not required for any results in the paper. The end-to-end REINS pipeline (calibration latent collection, classifier scoring, SPCA direction computation, and steered evaluation) for a 1.3B parameter T2V model completes in under 24 GPU-hours on this hardware. All non-generation components, SPCA computation, VideoAlign [31] scoring, and safety-classifier training, fit within the memory budget of an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 (24 GB) and were in fact developed and run on a single 3090. Software: PyTorch 2.4 with the Diffusers, Transformers, and PEFT libraries; mixed-precision is used for training the safety classifier.

C.2 Safety Classifier Training

Architecture:

The safety classifier is a temporal Transformer encoder applied on top of a frozen vision backbone. For each video, T=8T{=}8 uniformly sampled frames are encoded into a sequence of patch-level features with a frozen pretrained backbone (SigLIP [43]), d=768d{=}768). Sinusoidal positional embeddings are added along the temporal axis, and the resulting (T,d)(T,d) sequence is passed through a 44-layer multi-head self-attention encoder (88 heads, GELU, dropout 0.10.1). Tokens are mean-pooled across time and projected by a linear head to per-category logits passed through a sigmoid for multi-label prediction. Heads are sized to the dataset: 1313 classes for SafeSora [1] (safe + 12 unsafe categories) and 77 for SafeWatch-Bench [2] (safe + 6 unsafe categories).

Optimization:

The encoder and classification head are trained with AdamW (β1=0.9,β2=0.999\beta_{1}{=}0.9,\beta_{2}{=}0.999), per-GPU learning rate 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5} (linearly scaled by world size under DDP), weight decay 1×10−21{\times}10^{-2}, and gradient clipping at ‖g‖2≤1\|g\|_{2}\leq 1. The schedule is a 11-epoch linear warmup followed by cosine decay over 1010 total epochs. Per-device batch size is 1616 videos (⇒128\Rightarrow 128 frames per step at T=8T{=}8). The loss is binary cross-entropy with logits over the multi-label target. Training is conducted in autocast mixed precision; the backbone is held in eval mode and never updated. The seed is 4242. Checkpoints are selected by best accuracy on the held-out test split.

Data:

For SafeSora [1], we use the official 13-label annotations and the train/test split released with the dataset. For SafeWatch-Bench [2], we collapse the per-clip C1-C6 multi-hot annotations into the same multi-label format (plus a derived “safe” indicator).

C.3 REINS Calibration and Steering

Calibration:

For each backbone we record the post-block residual hidden states {Zt∈ℝN×τ×dh}t=0T−1\{Z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times\tau\times d_{h}}\}_{t=0}^{T-1} at the chosen steering layer over N=500N{=}500 calibration prompts (drawn from SafeSora “safety-critical” or SafeWatch-Bench “unsafe” depending on the experiment). We additionally record the safety classifier’s per-video prediction y∈[0,1]Cy\in[0,1]^{C}, where C=13C{=}13 (SafeSora) or 77 (SafeWatch).

Direction discovery (SPCA):

At each denoising step tt, we mean-pool ZtZ_{t} across the token axis to a per-sample vector in ℝdh\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}, center both the hidden states and the (scalar safe-class) labels, and form the cross-covariance C=(H​Zt)⊤​(H​y)C=(HZ_{t})^{\top}(Hy), where H=I−1N​𝟏𝟏⊤H=I-\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} is the centering matrix. We take the top-K=6K=6 left singular vectors of CC and combine them as a single weighted direction δt=∑i=1Kσi2ui/∥⋅∥2\delta_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sigma_{i}^{2}\,u_{i}/\|\cdot\|_{2}, following the rank-11 formulation as empirically validated in Sec. 3.

Steering hook:

A forward hook on the chosen transformer block ℓ\ell injects λ⋅δt\lambda\cdot\delta_{t} into the residual hidden state during the steering window [tstart,tend)[t_{\text{start}},t_{\text{end}}) (we use the first half, [0,α​T)[0,\alpha T), with α=0.5\alpha=0.5 throughout). To prevent magnitude drift and the resulting color shift we observed at large λ\lambda, the perturbed state is rescaled per channel to preserve its original L2L_{2} norm along the token axis (the channel norm-preservation mode in our hook). For models whose pipelines run conditional and unconditional CFG passes separately (Wan [4]), the hook fires twice per denoising step and the same delta is added to both branches to cancel CFG amplification; for models that batch CFG (CogVideoX [3], LTX [6], Mochi [5], Allegro [7]) the delta is added to both halves of the batched activation.

Evaluation:

We hold out a disjoint set of 500500 evaluation prompts, generate paired baseline and steered videos with the same per-prompt seed, and report (i) the safety rate of our temporal SigLIP classifier, (ii) Visual Quality (VQ)/Motion Quality (MQ) VideoAlign [31] metrics.

C.4 Per-Model Steering Configurations

Table A1 lists every video model on which we evaluate REINS, together with the exact generation hyperparameters and the optimal steering configuration we report in the main paper. “Layer” is the index of the transformer block whose post-block residual is steered (we always steer a single layer, chosen as the geometric middle of the backbone’s transformer stack as a default and tuned by sweep where necessary). λ⋆\lambda^{\star} is the steering strength selected via the lambda sweep described in Sec. 2; the steering window is [0,0.5​T)[0,0.5T) across all models, and the norm-preservation mode is channel throughout.

Common settings:

For every entry in Table A1 we use: N=500N{=}500 calibration prompts and 500500 paired evaluation prompts (disjoint from calibration set), top-K=6K{=}6 SPCA components per timestep aggregated into a rank-11 direction, steering window [tstart,tend)=[0,⌊0.5​Tsteps⌋)[t_{\text{start}},t_{\text{end}})=[0,\lfloor 0.5\,T_{\text{steps}}\rfloor), and channel-wise norm preservation. Random seeds are kept fixed and deterministic per prompt in both baseline and steered generation, ensuring paired comparison.

C.5 Adversarial-Prompt Robustness Setting

For the MMA-Diffusion robustness experiment (Sec. 3) we use the first 500500 rows of the public MMA-Diffusion adversarial NSFW prompt set. The Llama-Prompt-Guard-2 [32] baseline uses a malicious-class threshold of 0.50.5 on the softmax-normalized logits; blocked prompts contribute as “safe” (no video generated). REINS uses the precomputed Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [4] safety direction discovered on SafeSora [1] calibration data, i.e., this is a strict zero-shot test: the steering direction is never tuned on MMA-Diffusion [33] prompts. Per-prompt seeds match across all three conditions for paired comparison.

C.6 Reproducibility

Calibration latents, computed SPCA directions, and classifier checkpoints are all deterministic given a seed; we will release the codebase upon acceptance, the per-model configuration files, and the exact prompt indices used for both calibration and evaluation. The reported safety and VQ/MQ can be reproduced end-to-end from the released artifacts in under 24 GPU-hours per model on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada.

Appendix D Adapting Noise-Space Steering to Video Diffusion

PolyJuice [20] was originally proposed as a black-box red-teaming method for synthetic image detectors on text-to-image diffusion models. It identifies directions in the noise-space latent of an image diffusion model via supervised PCA on detector predictions, and adds these directions to the latent during sampling to evade detection. We adapt it as a baseline for safety alignment in video diffusion following Algorithm 1 of [20] as faithfully as possible; we document the adaptation here for reproducibility.

Variable of intervention:

The original method targets the noise-space latent 𝐱t∈ℝC×H′×W′\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}} that the scheduler updates between denoising steps in image diffusion. For video diffusion, the analogous variable is 𝐱t∈ℝC×F′×H′×W′\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times F^{\prime}\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}}, where F′F^{\prime} is the temporally compressed frame count. We flatten the spatio-temporal axes and treat each video as a D′=C⋅F′⋅H′⋅W′D^{\prime}=C\cdot F^{\prime}\cdot H^{\prime}\cdot W^{\prime}-dimensional sample. This treats temporal structure identically to spatial structure, mirroring how PolyJuice treats spatial structure in 2D latents.

Calibration data:

We use the same SafeSora calibration set as REINS: N=500N=500 generations from safety-critical prompts, paired with binary safety labels (or 7-class soft labels where available). For direct comparability, the labels and prompts are identical to those used for REINS’s direction discovery.

Per-timestep direction computation (Algorithm 1 of [20]):

Unlike REINS, which discovers a single direction at a chosen layer, PolyJuice computes a separate direction 𝜹t∈ℝD′\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D^{\prime}} at each denoising step tt. For each step, we stack the NN flattened latents into 𝐙t∈ℝN×D′\mathbf{Z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D^{\prime}}, center both 𝐙t\mathbf{Z}_{t} and the label matrix 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, and form the cross-covariance 𝐂t=𝐙t⊤​𝐇𝐘centered\mathbf{C}_{t}=\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}_{\text{centered}}. SVD of 𝐂t\mathbf{C}_{t} yields left singular vectors {Uk}\{U_{k}\} and singular values {sk}\{s_{k}\}, and the steering direction follows PolyJuice’s Eq. 4:

𝜹t=∑k=1Kσk⋅Uk,σk=sk2,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sigma_{k}\cdot U_{k},\qquad\sigma_{k}=s_{k}^{2}, (A7)

with K=2K=2. We then apply two post-processing steps. First, a sign-determination pass: we project all NN centered latents at the middle denoising step onto 𝜹T/2\boldsymbol{\delta}_{T/2} and flip the sign of every 𝜹t\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t} if the projection correlates negatively with the safe class, ensuring +λ+\lambda consistently steers toward safety. Second, each 𝜹t\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t} is normalized to unit norm.

Inference-time intervention:

The intervention adds λt⋅𝜹t\lambda_{t}\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t} to the noise-space latent at the end of each denoising step:

𝐱~t=𝐱t+λt⋅𝜹t,λt=λ⋅𝟏{a≤t/T<b},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\lambda_{t}\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t},\qquad\lambda_{t}=\lambda\cdot\mathbf{1}\{a\leq t/T<b\}, (A8)

following PolyJuice’s window-restricted form (§\lx@sectionsignA.4 of [20]). We use a=0a=0 and b=0.5b=0.5, matching the steering fraction of REINS for parity. No per-channel norm preservation is applied; REINS’s norm preservation is specific to hidden-state activations and would conflict with the diffusion variance schedule that governs 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}.

Strength sweep:

We sweep λ∈{0.5,1,2,5,10,25,50,100}\lambda\in\{0.5,1,2,5,10,25,50,100\} and select the value that maximizes safety rate without producing degenerate outputs. We observe a sharp transition: for λ≤5\lambda\leq 5, generations are visually indistinguishable from the baseline and safety rate is unchanged; for λ≥25\lambda\geq 25, generations collapse to single-color or noise frames (Fig. A1). No intermediate value of λ\lambda produces meaningful safety steering with intact generation. The numbers reported in Table 3 use λ=10\lambda=10, which lies in the narrow regime where some generations remain coherent but neither safety nor quality is consistently improved.

Interpretation:

The failure mode is consistent with the absence of linear semantic structure in 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. The noise-space latent is, by construction, a partially denoised video tensor whose statistics are dominated by the diffusion noise schedule rather than by the model’s semantic processing. SPCA on this tensor identifies the direction of maximal label-correlated variance, but that variance is dominated by low-level pixel statistics rather than by safety-relevant content. Steering along this direction therefore shifts low-level statistics (and at sufficient magnitude, breaks the latent’s distribution entirely) without redirecting the model’s semantic intent. This contrasts with hidden-state steering (Eq. 13), where 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} acts on a representation in which high-level concepts are linearly organized. [20] themselves acknowledge in their Sec. 7 that the linearity assumption is the most significant limitation of the approach; our finding is consistent with that limitation being more severe in the higher-dimensional video setting.

Appendix E Potential Defense Mechanisms against REINS

To mitigate the risk of bad actors weaponizing REINS to deliberately elicit harmful content, developers can implement countermeasures that target the underlying geometry of the model’s hidden states. Since the efficacy of REINS hinges on the linear separability of safe and unsafe generation trajectories, a natural defense is to actively disrupt this subspace. Techniques drawn from concept unlearning and invariant representation learning could be employed to intentionally collapse or entangle the boundary between these features. If the harmful representation manifold is structurally erased during the model’s safety fine-tuning phase, simple linear perturbations will no longer be able to reliably synthesize unsafe video, thereby neutralizing this specific attack vector.

Furthermore, the REINS methodology can be repurposed as a highly effective, automated red-teaming utility. Instead of relying on manual or heuristic prompt jailbreaks to test model vulnerabilities, developers can invert the REINS safety direction to systematically generate sophisticated adversarial samples. We strongly encourage practitioners to incorporate these machine-generated failure cases directly into their defensive training pipelines. Using these challenging videos as negative constraints for preference optimization techniques (such as DPO) or to train more resilient safety classifiers will ultimately fortify video diffusion models against representation-level manipulation.
